chapters.title: Chapter 2: Detecting Regimes: From Rules to Statistics

lessons.title: Rule-Based Regime Flags: Moving Averages and India VIX Thresholds

body.text: The simplest possible regime detector is one number and one threshold. It will not survive contact with Chapter 7's stress tests, but you need a working baseline before you are allowed to add complexity on top of it.

children.text: Chapter 1 built intuition: three dimensions, real episodes, and a sense of how long regimes persist. This chapter turns that intuition into code. Start with the crudest possible tools, moving average crossovers and India VIX bands, and you will see exactly where they hold up and exactly where they don't. That gap is precisely what Hidden Markov Models in Chapter 3 exist to close.
A Trend Flag: The 50/200-Day Moving Average, Repurposed

In Lesson 1 of Chapter 1, the 50/200-day crossover was a standalone strategy: buy when it flips up, sell when it flips down. Here it plays a different role. It becomes a trend flag, a single label attached to every trading day, that other strategies can read before deciding whether to trade at all. The computation is identical; the use is not.

body.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# nifty_df: daily closes for Nifty 50, indexed by date, sorted ascending
nifty_df['sma_50'] = nifty_df['close'].rolling(window=50).mean()
nifty_df['sma_200'] = nifty_df['close'].rolling(window=200).mean()

nifty_df['trend_flag'] = np.where(
    nifty_df['sma_50'] > nifty_df['sma_200'], 'up', 'down'
)

# First ~200 rows have no 200-day SMA yet; they are not a real signal
nifty_df = nifty_df.dropna(subset=['sma_50', 'sma_200'])
body.caption: A daily trend flag, derived the same way as the Chapter 1 crossover system, now used as a label rather than a trade signal

children.text: A Volatility Flag: India VIX Bands

India VIX gives you the volatility dimension directly, without computing realized volatility yourself. A common, simple convention is to split it into four bands. These thresholds are a starting convention, not a law of markets; treat them as adjustable parameters you will revisit once you have more data to work with in later chapters.

body.caption: A simple India VIX banding convention

cells: Calm; typical of a settled uptrend
Ordinary market conditions, no elevated stress
Real but contained stress, e.g. the 2022 rate-hike cycle
Crisis-level stress; the March 2020 spike went well beyond even this band

body.caption: Banding India VIX into a discrete volatility flag

children.text: Combining Two Flags Into a Regime Grid

Two flags, trend and volatility, combine into a grid of named regimes. Collapse the four VIX bands to two coarse buckets, low or normal versus elevated or extreme, and you get four cells that map cleanly onto the archetypes from Chapter 1.

body.caption: A trend flag times a coarse volatility flag, mapped to Chapter 1's archetypes

body.code:
regime_df = nifty_df[['trend_flag']].join(vix_df[['vol_flag']], how='inner')

regime_map = {
    ('up', 'low'):        'Calm Uptrend',
    ('up', 'normal'):     'Calm Uptrend',
    ('up', 'elevated'):   'Volatile Whipsaw',
    ('up', 'extreme'):    'Volatile Whipsaw',
    ('down', 'low'):      'Range-Bound Chop',
    ('down', 'normal'):   'Range-Bound Chop',
    ('down', 'elevated'): 'Volatile Whipsaw',
    ('down', 'extreme'):  'Panic Selloff',
}

regime_df['regime'] = regime_df.apply(
    lambda row: regime_map[(row['trend_flag'], row['vol_flag'])], axis=1
)
body.caption: Combining the trend and volatility flags into a single daily regime label

body.text: Notice what the code makes explicit that a chart never would: 'up' plus 'extreme' is labelled Volatile Whipsaw, not Calm Uptrend, and 'down' plus 'elevated' also lands on Volatile Whipsaw rather than a clean Panic Selloff. Trend and volatility really are independent dials, exactly as Chapter 1 argued, and the regime_map has to encode that independence by hand because a single moving average or a single VIX threshold cannot express it alone.

children.text: Where This Simple Grid Already Breaks

Look closely at the 'down, low or normal' cell. It is labelled Range-Bound Chop, but a genuine down trend with calm volatility, a slow, orderly bear market, is a real regime that is not one of Chapter 1's four archetypes at all. The grid forces it into the nearest available label because a four-cell table only has four labels to give. That is not a bug you fix by adding a fifth row. It is a structural limit of rule-based flags: every threshold you pick draws a hard line through what is actually a continuous, multi-dimensional space, and somewhere that line will cut through a regime that deserved its own label.

body.text: There is a second, sharper problem waiting at every threshold boundary. If India VIX drifts between 19 and 21 for a week, this code flips vol_flag between 'normal' and 'elevated' on every small move, and regime_df['regime'] flips with it. That is a whipsaw inside the detector itself, distinct from the strategy whipsaw in Chapter 1 but caused by the exact same problem: a hard binary decision applied to a noisy, continuous quantity. Lesson 3 of this chapter measures exactly how often this happens and what it costs.

body.title: Build the Two-Flag Pipeline on Real Data
steps: Download Nifty 50 daily closing prices for at least the last three years, from NSE historical data or a data vendor of your choice
Download matching India VIX daily closing levels for the same date range
Compute sma_50, sma_200, and trend_flag exactly as shown in this lesson
Apply the vix_band function to derive vol_flag from the India VIX series
Join trend_flag and vol_flag on date and apply regime_map to produce a daily regime label
Plot the resulting regime label as background shading behind the Nifty price chart and visually check it against the 2020 and 2022 episodes from Chapter 1

body.title: Reading the Regime Map
body.question: According to the regime_map in this lesson, what label does trend_flag = 'up' combined with vol_flag = 'extreme' (India VIX above 30) produce?
options: 'Panic Selloff', since extreme volatility always means panic
'Volatile Whipsaw', a trending market with unusually high volatility
'Calm Uptrend', since the trend flag is still 'up'
'Range-Bound Chop', since high volatility implies no clear direction
body.explanation: The regime_map treats trend and volatility as independent, so an up trend combined with extreme volatility lands on 'Volatile Whipsaw', not 'Calm Uptrend' or 'Panic Selloff'. This is the same point from Chapter 1's comparison of a calm uptrend against a volatile, trending selloff: direction alone never tells you the full regime.

points: A trend flag reuses the Chapter 1 crossover computation, but as a label read by other logic rather than a standalone trade signal
India VIX bands turn the volatility dimension into a simple, discrete flag without needing to compute realized volatility directly

Combining a trend flag and a coarse volatility flag into a grid recovers the four archetypes from Chapter 1, but forces every regime that doesn't fit one of the four cells into the nearest available label
Hard thresholds create whipsaws inside the detector itself whenever the underlying series drifts across a boundary repeatedly
These limitations are not implementation bugs; they are structural limits of rule-based detection, and they are exactly what Lesson 3 measures and Chapter 3's statistical models are built to address
